'''''Radiola linoides''''' is the sole species in the '''''Radiola''''' genus, a [[monotypic]] genus of [[flowering plant]]s belonging to the family [[Linaceae]]. It has the common names of 'allseed' and 'flaxseed'. It has a very short stem which is repeatedly subdivided, with a pair of very small leaves and a single white flower at each fork and at the end of the branches. It has leaves which are opposite arranged, oval (in shape) and sessile.

==Description==
[[File:Radiola linoides sl18.jpg|thumb|right|Flower bud of ''Radiola linoides'', Czech Republic]]
''Radiola linoides'' is a small,<ref name=Readers/><ref name="dorset"/><ref name="habitas"/> [[Herbaceous plant|herbaceous]],<ref name="FNA"/> [[Annual plant|annual]].<ref name="habitas"/><ref name=Anatomic/><ref name=Poland/><!-- also <ref name="dorset"> --> It is commonly overlooked due to its size,<ref name="dorset"/> and delicate form.<ref name=Readers/>
It is between {{convert|1.3|-|7.5|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall,<ref name=Readers/><ref name=Anatomic/><ref name=Poland/><!-- also <ref name="FNA"/>--> and [[dichotomously]] branched,<ref name="FNA"/><ref name=Sowerby/> (meaning dividing at [[axils]] into 2 branches), repeatedly subdivided,<ref name=Murray/> or forked.<ref name=Poland/><ref name=Gray/><ref name="habitas"/> The hairless,<ref name="dorset"/> stems are very slender,<ref name=Anatomic/> threadlike,<ref name="dorset"/><ref name=Sowerby/> about 0.5 mm in diameter.<ref name=Poland/> They are often purple-flushed,<ref name=Poland/> or reddish.<ref name="dorset"/>

The leaves are arranged [[Phyllotaxis|opposite]],<ref name=Gray/><ref name=Anatomic/><ref name=Murray/><!-- also <ref name="habitas"/><ref name=Poland/><ref name="dorset"/><ref name=Readers/>--> and are obovate,<ref name=Poland/> or ovate to elliptic in form.<ref name=Anatomic/><ref name=Gray/><ref name=Poland/> They are very small,<ref name=Poland/><ref name=Murray/> only {{convert|1.5|-|2|mm|0|abbr=on}} long and dull green or slightly glaucous, often tinged with purple and quite glabrous (hairless).<ref name=Sowerby/> They have one-vein,<ref name="dorset"/> and have transparent (or [[hyaline]]) margins that appear ragged due to the presence of minute teeth or lobes along the edges.<ref name=Poland/><ref name="Stace2010"/>

It has [[bracts]] which are usually leaf-like.<ref name="FNA"/> 
It flowers between July and August,<ref name=Gray/><ref name="FNA"/><ref name="dorset"/><!-- also <ref name=Readers/> --> with numerous tiny flowers,<ref name=Sowerby/><ref name=Stroh/><ref name=Poland/><!-- also <ref name="dorset"/><ref name=Anatomic/> --> at the branch tips,<ref name=Readers/><ref name=Arber/> or at each forked stem.<ref name=Murray/> They are white,<ref name=Anatomic/> with 4 equal,<ref name="FNA"/><ref name=Poland/><ref name=Sowerby/><!-- also <ref name="habitas"/> --> [[sepals]] and 4 [[petals]].<ref name=Jacob/><ref name=Sowerby/> They are {{convert|1.0|-|1.5|mm|0|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="FNA"/><ref name=Stroh/>

It has 4 stamens,<ref name=Gray/> which are {{convert|0.5|-|0.8|mm|0|abbr=on}} long<ref name="FNA"/> and white [[anthers]].<ref name="FNA"/> 
The very small [[pollen]] of the plant has been analysed and measured to be about 25μm.<ref>W. Punt and G.C.S. Clarke (Editors) {{google books|XUSPDAAAQBAJ|The Northwest European Pollen Flora: Reprinted from Review of Palaeobotany and Palynology Vol.33 (2016)|page=86}}</ref>

After flowering, it produces a seed capsule, which is rounded,<ref name=Anatomic/> or globular.<ref name=Readers/><ref name=Sowerby/>
The globose seed capsules are thought to be more noticeable than the flowers.<ref name="dorset"/> The common name of 'allseed' is due to the multiple seed capsules on the plant, each containing 8 seeds.<ref name=Murray/> The seed capsules are 0.1 mm wide,<ref name=Stroh/> and have 8 cells and 8 valves.<ref name=Jacob/><ref name=Sowerby/> Inside the capsules, are very small, ({{convert|0.4|-|0.5|mm|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|0.2|-|0.3|mm|0|abbr=on}} wide) brown seeds, that are obovoid to ellipsoid in shape. They are slightly flattened on one side and have a smooth, lustrous surface.<ref name=Stroh/><ref name=Bojňanský2007/>

===Ploidy===
It has a chromosome reading of 2n = 18.<ref name="FNA"/>

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Flora of Syria, Palestine, and Sinai - from the Taurus to Ras Muhammas and from the Mediterranean sea to the Syrian desert (1896) (14761607966).jpg|thumb|Illustration from Flora of Syria by George Edward Post, in 1838-1909]]
It has several common names including; 'allseed',<ref name=Readers/><ref name=Arber/><ref name="RHS">{{cite web |title=''Radiola linoides'' {{!}} allseed /RHS Gardening |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/160801/radiola-linoides/details |website=www.rhs.org.uk |access-date=28 December 2021 |language=en-gb}}</ref><!-- also <ref name="dorset"/><ref name=GRIN/><ref name=Murray/> --> this is due to its ability to have multiple seed production.<ref name=Readers/>
It is also known as 'flax seed',<ref name=Sowerby/><ref name="RHS"/> 'thyme leaved flaxseed',<ref name=Murray/> and 'thousand seeded flax'.<ref name=Gray/>

In Swedish, it is known as 'dvärglin'.<ref name=GRIN/>

It was originally named and published as ''Linum radiola'' by [[Linnaeus]] in his book [[Sp. Pl.]] on page 281 in 1753.<ref name=Griffiths>Ralph Griffiths and George Edward Griffiths (Editors) {{google books|P0xQAQAAMAAJ|The Monthly Review, Volume 34 (1801)|page=56}}</ref><ref name=Naqshi>A.R. Naqshi {{google books|yiMsEAAAQBAJ|An Introduction to Botanical Nomenclature (2019)|page=73}}</ref> Then in 1756, [[John Hill (botanist)|Hill]] transferred it into the genus ''Radiola'', it also assumed the name ''Radiola radiola''. Although being a [[tautonym]], it was declared not valid by taxonomists.<ref name=Naqshi/> So then in 1788, Roth gave the species name as ''Radiola linoides''.<ref name=Naqshi/><ref name=Griffiths/>

The genus of ''Radiola'' has one known synonym of ''Millegrana'' {{small|Adans.}},<ref name="POWO"/> when the species was known as ''Millegrana radiola'' {{small|Druce}}, Fl. Berks. 114 in 1898.<ref>{{cite web |title=''Millegrana radiola'' {{!}} International Plant Names Index |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/544801-1 |website=www.ipni.org |access-date=8 January 2022}}</ref>

The genus ''Radiola'' was first described and published in John Hill's book, 'The British Herbal' on page 227 in 1756,<ref name="POWO"/> and then later the species ''Radiola linoides'' was first published by [[Albrecht Wilhelm Roth]] in Tentamen Florae Germanicae (Tent. Fl. Germ.) Vol.1 on page 71 in 1788.<ref name=Species>{{cite web |title=''Radiola linoides'' |url=https://www.ipni.org/n/544861-1 |website=www.ipni.org |publisher=[[International Plant Names Index]] |access-date=28 December 2021}}</ref>

The genus name of ''Radiola'' is derived from the Latin word ''radius'' meaning a ray, because the cells of the ripe capsule diverge like a little wheel.<ref name=Jacob/> The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] of ''linoides'' is derived from ''Linum'' (from the original Linnaeus name of ''Linum radiola'').<ref name=Griffiths/>

The genus and species is recognized by the [[United States Department of Agriculture]] and the [[Agricultural Research Service]], since 3 February 1998.<ref name=GRIN>{{cite web |title=Taxon: Radiola linoides Roth |url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxon/taxonomygenus?id=410122 |website=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov |access-date=8 January 2022}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Radiola linoides sl9.jpg|thumb|right|''Radiola linoides'' on the shore of a pond, Jihočeský kraj, [[Czech Republic]]]]

===Range===
Its wide native range stretches from temperate Europe,<ref name=Anatomic/> (found within the countries of Albania, the Balearic Islands, the Baltic States (such as Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania), Belarus, Belgium, Bulgaria, Corsica, Czechoslovakia, Denmark, France, Germany, Great Britain (including [[Northern Ireland]]<ref name="habitas">{{cite web |title=''Radiola linoides'' Roth - Allseed :: Flora of Northern Ireland |url=http://www.habitas.org.uk/flora/species.asp?item=3146 |website=www.habitas.org.uk |access-date=3 January 2022}}</ref>), Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Portugal, Romania, Sardinia, Sicily, Spain, Sweden, Ukraine and Yugoslavia), parts of Russia (including; [[European Russia|central European Russia]], northwest European Russia and south European Russia), [[Macaronesia]] (including; the Canary Islands, [[Cape Verde]] and [[Madeira]]), parts of Africa (including; Algeria, Cameroon, Ethiopia, Madagascar, Malawi, Morocco (including the [[Tingitan Peninsula]],<ref>Lund Botanical Society {{google books|POJOAAAAMAAJ|Botaniska Notiser 1972, Vol 125|page=448}}</ref>), Tanzania and Tunisia),<ref>{{cite book |last1=Leistner |first1=O.A. |title=Seed plants of southern tropical Africa: families and genera. |date=2005 |publisher=South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI Publishing) |isbn=9781919976075 |chapter=Southern African Botanical Diversity Network Report No. 26.}}</ref> and also parts of western Asia (including; Lebanon, Syria and Turkey).<ref name="POWO"/><ref name=GRIN/>

It was later introduced into America and found in [[Maine]], [[New Brunswick]] and [[Nova Scotia]].<ref name="POWO"/> It was introduced to New Zealand, on North Island ([[Kaimaumau wetland|Kaimaumau Swamp]]).<ref>{{cite web |title=''Radiola linoides'' |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora/species/radiola-linoides/ |website=New Zealand Plant Conservation Network |access-date=28 September 2023 |language=en}}</ref>

It was found to be [[Extinction|extinct]] in Switzerland,<ref name="POWO"/><ref name=infoflora/><ref>Państwowe Wydawn {{google books|maVKAAAAYAAJ|FFG, Volumes 43-44 (1998)}}</ref> and is listed as being rare in [[Lithuania]].<ref name=Marciniuk/>

===Habitat===
It is a [[calcifuge]] species (meaning it does not tolerate alkaline soils),<ref name=Stroh/> and it grows on [[Acidic soil|acidic]] and damp soils, in grasslands and [[heaths]],<ref name=Readers/> and [[Common land|commons]],<ref name=Sowerby/> or beside ponds, paths,<ref name="dorset"/> or tracks and in woodland rides,<ref name="plantatlas"/> and on roadsides (in Scotland).<ref name=Murray/> In southern England, it can also be found on the margins of fishponds, fields or abandoned meadows and old sand pits,<ref name=Anatomic/> and moist, boggy places in [[Devon]].<ref name=Jacob/> It likes the damp forests on the Iberian Peninsula.<ref>Javier Loidi (Editor) {{google books|f6U2DwAAQBAJ|The Vegetation of the Iberian Peninsula: Volume 2 (2017)|page=388}}</ref> Tolerating [[Soil fertility|infertile]], peaty or sandy ground.<ref name="FNA"/><ref name="dorset"/> Near the coast, it is found in [[Interdunal wetland|dune slacks]],<ref name=Anatomic/><ref>Christoph Leuschner and Heinz Ellenberg {{google books|j7I1DwAAQBAJ|Ecology of Central European Non-Forest Vegetation: Coastal to Alpine, Natural to Man-made Habitats, Volume 2 (2017) |page=84}}</ref> sandy grassland, on [[machair]], and in soil-filled rock cracks,<ref name="plantatlas"/> or rocky outcrops.<ref name="FNA"/>
It is found at [[altitudes]] of between {{convert|0|to|100|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level.<ref name="FNA"/>

==Ecology==
[[File:Radiola linoides 219375813.jpg|thumb|right|Allseed (''Radiola linoides''), Netherlands]]

In Britain, it is generally found in acidic grasslands and [[heathlands]],<ref name=Readers/> on grassy cliff slopes, along the rutted (broken) edges of tracks, beside woodland rides and firebreaks, at the edges of ponds, in sandy grassland, [[machair]] (low-lying grassy plains) and dune slacks and in soil-filled rock crevices (Wilmore 2002;<ref>{{cite book |last1=Wilmore |editor1-last=Preston |editor1-first=C.D. |editor2-last=Pearman |editor2-first=D.A. |editor3-last=Dines |editor3-first=T.D. |title=New Atlas of the British and Irish Flora. |date=2002 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford. |page=436 |chapter=''Radiola linoides'' Roth.}}</ref> Chater 2010;<ref>{{cite book |last1=Chater |first1=A.O. |title=Flora of Cardiganshire. |date=2010 |publisher=Privately published |location=Aberystwyth}}</ref> Rand & Mundell 2011).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rand |first1=M. |last2=Mundell |first2=T. |title=Hampshire Rare Plant Register. |date=2011 |publisher=Trollius Publications. |isbn=9780953971848}}</ref> In [[Dorset]], it is often found with Chaffweed (''[[Anagallis minima]]'').<ref name="dorset"/>

''Radiola linoides'' is a plant of sparsely vegetated, damp, infertile, moderately acid peaty, gravelly or sandy soils, often found in draw-down zones or where there has been some poaching by livestock.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Edwards |first1=B. |last2=Pearman |first2=D.A. |title=Dorset Rare Plant Register. |date=2004 |publisher=Henry Ling Ltd. |location=Dorchester.}}</ref> Rodwell in 2000, included ''R. linoides'' as an associate of short open turf belonging to the [[British National Vegetation Classification|NVC]], [[British NVC community MC5|MC5]], maritime therophyte community but its NVC affinities are likely to be much broader and include a range of grassland and heathland types.<ref name=Rodwell2000>{{cite book |editor1-last=Rodwell |editor1-first=J.S. |title=British Plant Communities Volume 5 – Maritime Communities and Vegetation of Open Habitats |date=2000 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |location=Cambridge. |isbn=0-521-64476-3 |edition=5}}</ref>

Whilst in Ireland, it is found growing with ''[[Plantago maritima]]'' in dense, exposed conditions.<ref>[[Arthur Tansley|Sir Arthur George Tansley]] {{google books|Dis8AAAAIAAJ|The British Islands and Their Vegetation, Volume 2 (1949)|page=901}}</ref>

It grows in Poland, with other damp loving plants such as ''[[Cyperus flavescens]]'', ''[[Centunculus minimus]]'' and ''[[Illecebrum verticillatum]]''.<ref name=Marciniuk>{{cite journal |last1=Marciniuk |first1=Paweł |last2=Marciniuk |first2=Jolanta |last3=Łysko |first3=Andrzej |last4=Krajewski |first4=Łukasz |last5=Chudecka |first5=Justyna |last6=Skrzyczyńska |first6=Janina |last7=Popiela |first7=Agnieszka Anna |title=Rediscovery of ''Cyperus flavescens'' (''Cyperaceae'') on the northeast periphery of its range in Europe |journal=PeerJ |date=14 September 2020 |volume=8|article-number=e9837 |doi=10.7717/peerj.9837 |doi-access=free |pmid=32983639 |pmc=7497605 }}</ref>

Across Europe, ''R. linoides'' is also associated with annual-rich west Mediterranean siliceous grassland, the [[fumaroles]] of [[Pantelleria]] in Sicily, ''[[Juncus bufonius]]'' dominated communities with ''[[Centunculus minimus]]'' and ''[[Centaurium pulchellum]]'', and temporarily inundated small herb communities with associates including Elatine spp., ''[[Damasonium bourgaei]]'' and ''[[Samolus valerandi]]'' (Anon 2013).<ref>{{cite book |title=Interpretation manual of European Union habitats EUR 28. |date=2013 |publisher=European Commission, DG Environment, Nature and biodiversity |location=Brussels. |page=144}}</ref> In the Netherlands, ''R. linoides'' was recorded from fields that are filled with water during the winter months and then frozen for ice skating.<ref name=Bojňanský2007>{{cite book |last1=Bojňanský |first1=V. |last2=Fargašová |first2=A. |title=Atlas of seed and fruits of Central and East-European Flora - The Carpathian Mountains region |date=2007 |publisher=Springer |location=The Netherlands. |isbn=978-94-017-7670-7}}</ref>

===Seed survival===
The seeds of ''R. linoides'' are able to survive in the soil, even after general situation conditions have become unsuitable for mature plants to establish in the above-ground vegetation (Plassmann et al. 2009). ''R. linoides'' is therefore capable of opportunistically colonising areas from the seed bank when suitable conditions (e.g. bare, damp, open ground) become available, although it is not known how long the seed remains viable if unsuitable conditions continue for an extended or prolonged period of time (i.e. more than five years).<ref name="Plassman2009">{{cite journal |last1=Plassmann |first1=K. |last2=Brown |first2=N. |last3=Jones |first3=M.L. |last4=Edwards-Jones |first4=G. |title=Can soil seed banks contribute to the restoration of dune slacks under conservation management? |journal=Applied Vegetation Science |date=2009 |volume=12 |issue=2 |pages=199–210|doi=10.1111/j.1654-109X.2009.01014.x |bibcode=2009AppVS..12..199P }}</ref>

The very small, smooth seeds are also known to be able to survive internal ([[endozoochorous]]) dispersal by animals, and the combination of seed morphology and habitat suggests that ''R. linoides'' seed also has the potential to be transported long distances on the feet or feathers of wildfowl (Salisbury 1970),<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Salisbury |first1=E. |title=The Pioneer Vegetation of Exposed Mud and its Biological Features. |journal=[[Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London]] |date=1970 |volume=259 |issue=829 |pages=207–255|doi=10.1098/rstb.1970.0059 |bibcode=1970RSPTB.259..207S }}</ref> or on the feet or hair of cattle.<ref name=Stroh/>

==Pests==
''Radiola linoides'' has been recorded as a host for ''[[Melampsora lini]]'', a fungal pathogen responsible for [[Rust (fungus)|rust disease]] on flax and linseed plants. (Lawrence et al. 2007)<ref name="Lawrence2007">{{cite journal |last1=Lawrence |first1=G.J. |last2=Dodds |first2=P.N. |last3=Ellis |first3=J.G. |title=Rust of flax and linseed caused by ''Melampsora lini''. |journal=Molecular Plant Pathology |date=2007 |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=349–364|doi=10.1111/j.1364-3703.2007.00405.x |pmid=20507505 |bibcode=2007MolPP...8..349L }}</ref>

==Conservation==
Up to 1930, the population of ''R. linoides'' within the United Kingdom, went through a sharp decline in numbers of plants. This was mainly due to loss of habitat, (e.g. lowland heaths) or disturbances/damage to the habitats and also the lack of grazing (which in turn, increased the growth of more vigorous plants). It was estimated that up to 95% of a sample of sites in Dorset between 1935 and 1992 were lost and that remaining populations of the plant were very small.<ref name="dorset"/> It has a mainly coastal distribution across western Ireland, south-west England and Wales, northwards along the coast to western and north-east Scotland, with outliers in southern England and East Anglia. Its distribution within the rest of the British isles seemed to be stable. It could also be easily overlooked and may be under-recorded in some areas.<ref name="plantatlas">{{cite web |title=''Radiola linoides'' {{!}} Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/radiola-linoides |website=www.brc.ac.uk |access-date=28 December 2021 |language=en}}</ref> It was assessed in 2015, as [[Near Threatened]] in Great Britain as a whole, [[Vulnerable species|Vulnerable]] in England, but of [[Least Concern]] in [[Wales]].<ref name=Stroh/>

In Germany, the [[Venus flytrap]]s (''Dionaea muscipula'') was introduced into the Wahner Heide Nature Reserve near [[Bonn]] where a small population of the threatened ''Radiola linoides'' was mistakenly destroyed by conservationists when re-planting, before the introduced species was later removed.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cross |first1=Adam T. |last2=Krueger |first2=Thilo A. |last3=Gonella |first3=Paulo M. |last4=Robinson |first4=Alastair S. |last5=Fleischmann |first5=Andreas S. |title=Conservation of carnivorous plants in the age of extinction |journal=Global Ecology and Conservation |date=December 2020 |volume=24|article-number=e01272 |doi=10.1016/j.gecco.2020.e01272 |bibcode=2020GEcoC..2401272C |hdl=20.500.11937/84611 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>

In the biogeographic regions of [[Mittelland, Switzerland]] and Alpensüdflanke, it has been assessed as 'Regionally Extinct'.<ref name=infoflora>{{cite web |title=Species information |url=https://www.infoflora.ch/en/flora/radiola-linoides.html |website=www.infoflora.ch |access-date=28 September 2023}}</ref>

In the [[Czech Republic]], on the Red List 2017 (IUCN threat category) it is classed as CR - critically endangered, but since it was also classed as not a native plant, it is not protected.<ref>{{cite web |title=Pladias: Databáze české flóry a vegetace |url=https://pladias.cz/taxon/data/Radiola%20linoides |website=pladias.cz |access-date=28 September 2023}}</ref>
